passage: In the open-plan office of the ad agency, Jatin's screen lit up with a message from Ramesh: "WE GOT THE CLIENT!!!" Jatin grinned, because Ramesh always typed in capitals when thrilled. Ten minutes later the same manager pinged the whole team: "WHY IS THE FILE STILL NOT SENT???" Jatin's stomach dropped. Was that anger or panic? Nobody in the room could tell. Ramesh, at the next desk, caught Jatin's eye and said, "Should we ask her what she needs?" They walked over. It turned out she was terrified the client would leave and needed the file in an hour. Jatin sent it in twenty minutes and exhaled.

qa.q: What did Ramesh's first message say?
qa.a: Ramesh's message said "WE GOT THE CLIENT!!!"

qa.q: What did Jatin feel when the manager's capitals arrived, and what did they turn out to mean?
qa.a: Jatin's stomach dropped and Jatin could not tell if the capitals meant anger or panic. It turned out the manager was terrified of losing the client.

qa.q: What helped clear up the tone of the message?
qa.a: Ramesh suggested asking the manager what was needed, and a short walk over cleared it up.

qa.q: How might the manager have felt when the team seemed to hesitate?
qa.a: The manager was probably stressed and rushed and may not have noticed how the capitals sounded to others.

grounding: Illustrates ALL CAPS and many exclamation marks read as either excitement or anger, cleared up by asking directly.

Dear Nandini,

I got your voice note yesterday and, honestly, I thought you were furious. You were loud, fast, and your voice cracked on "how could you". I nearly wrote back angrily. Then I remembered that you shout when you are excited, and you had also just come from the match. So I called instead, and it turned out you were thrilled about the office move and wanted to tell me all at once! I laughed. I was so relieved I did not fire off a nasty reply. Next time I will ask before assuming, and please tell me when you are only excited. 🙂

Farida

qa.q: What did Farida do instead of writing back angrily?
qa.a: Farida called Nandini instead.

qa.q: What did Farida first think of Nandini's loud voice note, and what was the truth?
qa.a: Farida thought Nandini was furious, but Nandini was actually thrilled about the office move. Loud and fast voices can carry excitement or anger, so Farida checked.

qa.q: What did Farida do that avoided a quarrel?
qa.a: Farida called and asked instead of replying angrily, and offered to ask before assuming next time.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt on hearing Farida had thought that?
qa.a: Nandini might have felt surprised and a bit sorry, having only meant to share excitement.

grounding: Letter about a loud, fast voice note read as anger but meant as excitement, cleared up by a quick call.

passage: So, Shankar, you'll laugh. Tuesday night, eleven o'clock, my phone lights up. My manager, Mrs. Rego: "WHO SENT THE FINAL DECK TO THE CLIENT????" All caps. Four question marks. I sent it. I sat on my bed with my heart hammering, drafting apologies. Had I sent the wrong version? Missed a slide? I nearly typed, "I'm so sorry, it was me, I'll fix it." Then I thought: all caps could mean screaming-angry or screaming-happy. I don't actually know which. So I called her instead. She picked up laughing. "Kiran! Was it you? They LOVED it. They want to sign on Friday!" Twenty minutes of panic over four question marks. Now I call before drafting any apology, and I've told Mrs. Rego that her caps nearly gave me a heart attack.

qa.q: When did Mrs. Rego's message arrive?
qa.a: At eleven o'clock on Tuesday night.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling while drafting apologies?
qa.a: Kiran felt panicked and anxious, heart hammering, assuming the all-caps message meant anger over a mistake.

qa.q: What stopped the panic from going further?
qa.a: Kiran realised all caps could mean anger or excitement and called Mrs. Rego instead of sending an apology based on a guess.

qa.q: How was Mrs. Rego feeling when she sent the message?
qa.a: She was thrilled and excited because the client loved the deck; the caps and question marks carried her excitement.

grounding: Shows a young professional reading an all-caps message as anger when it was excitement, and a quick call clearing it up.

passage: I'm Imran, Tushar's flatmate. On Saturday evening he played a voice note from his cousin Rhea on speaker while we were cooking. It was loud: "TUSHAR! WHERE ARE YOU? WE'VE BEEN WAITING! CALL ME RIGHT NOW!" Behind her there was a roaring, crashing noise. Tushar went pale. "She's furious," he said. "I said I might come to the sangeet and then I forgot." He started typing a long apology. Honestly, I couldn't tell either. It sounded like shouting, but people shout for lots of reasons. I said, "Maybe just call?" He hesitated, then did. When she answered, the same roar came through, and she was laughing. "The dhol is right next to me! I'm not angry, silly, I just want you here for the dance!" Tushar put the half-written apology away and went looking for his kurta.

qa.q: What did Rhea's voice note ask Tushar to do?
qa.a: To call her right now, because they had been waiting.

qa.q: What did Tushar think Rhea's loud voice note meant?
qa.a: Tushar felt guilty and anxious, sure she was furious because he had forgotten the sangeet.

qa.q: Why was calling better than sending the long apology?
qa.a: A call let him hear her real tone, laughing over the dhol, and avoided apologising for anger that wasn't there.

qa.q: How did Imran read the voice note?
qa.a: Imran couldn't tell either; it sounded like shouting, but people shout for many reasons, so Imran suggested calling.

grounding: An observer describes a shouted voice note read as anger when it was excitement over loud music, and a call checking the tone.

Tuesday: Over lunch, Hafsa said quietly, "I wasn't blaming you yesterday. I type in caps when I'm stressed. Or excited. My whole family does." Pema winced. "I read it as shouting at me. Sorry for snapping."
The following Wednesday: "PEMA. THE CLIENT DEMO. CALL ME." Pema's stomach lurched out of habit. This time she didn't type anything. She just rang. Hafsa picked up, breathless. "They want to extend the contract! I had to tell someone!" Pema laughed, relieved. "Next time add a smiley so my heart survives." "No promises."

qa.q: What did Hafsa's Monday message say?
qa.a: "THE BUILD FAILED AGAIN!!!"

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when she read Monday's message?
qa.a: Pema felt defensive and a bit hurt, reading the caps as shouting and blame for her code; it was really Hafsa's stress.

qa.q: What did Pema do differently the following Wednesday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Instead of typing a reply to a guessed tone, Pema called straight away, which revealed excitement and avoided another quarrel.

qa.a: Hafsa likely felt hurt and misread, since she wasn't blaming anyone, which may explain the hour of silence.

grounding: Shows all-caps messages read as anger when they carried stress or excitement, and a quick call replacing a needless quarrel.

passage:
Sunaina, sit, I'll tell you why I never fight over a chat message. Years ago, when our office first got group chats, I was on leave for my sister's wedding. My boss, old Mr. Dutta, sent a voice note, shouting over traffic: "Binita! Call me. The Kolkata client! Call me NOW!" Then a text: "WHERE ARE YOU!!!"
My heart nearly stopped. I was sure I had ruined the account. I typed a long, defensive reply listing everything I had done, and my thumb was on send.
Then my sister said, "Didi, just call him." So I did. He was laughing. The client had signed for three years, and he wanted me to hear it first.
Capitals, exclamation marks, a loud voice in a street; they can be joy or rage. I still call before I reply. You try it too.

qa.q: Where was Binita when the voice note came?
qa.a: Binita was on leave for her sister's wedding.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when the voice note and text arrived?
qa.a: Binita felt panicked and afraid, sure the account was ruined, reading the shouting and capitals as anger when they were really excitement.

qa.q: What turning point stopped Binita from sending the defensive reply?
qa.a: Her sister said, "Didi, just call him," and Binita phoned Mr. Dutta instead of pressing send.

qa.q: How was Mr. Dutta feeling when he shouted into the voice note?
qa.a: He was excited and happy about the three-year deal and wanted Binita to hear it first; the shouting came from joy and traffic noise, not anger.

grounding: All caps, many exclamation marks and a shouted voice note can mean excitement or anger, and a quick call avoids a needless quarrel.
